ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left side of the figure, the AC power source Vs(t) is connected to the primary side of the transformer, and the transformer is labeled n:1. On the right side, the secondary side has a center tap, and the center tap is connected to the left end of the load resistor RL; the upper and lower ends of the secondary side are respectively connected through ideal diodes D1 and D2 to the common output terminal on the right side, and the load voltage VL(t) is labeled as negative on the left end and positive on the right end. Therefore this circuit is an ideal center-tapped full-wave rectifier circuit. Then reason: the input primary-side voltage is Vs(t)=10 sin(ωt), so the primary-side peak value is 10 V. The transformer is n:1 step-down, and this ratio corresponds to the entire secondary winding, so the peak value of the entire secondary side is 10/n V. Since the secondary side is a center-tapped structure, the peak value of each half of the secondary winding is 5/n V. After full-wave rectification, the load voltage is the full-wave rectified waveform of the half-secondary-winding voltage, whose average value is 2Vm/π, where Vm=5/n. Therefore VL,avg = 2(5/n)/π = 10/(nπ). The average value is known to be 2.5/π, so 10/(nπ)=2.5/π, solving gives n=4.
